tools.name: estimate_instance_cost
tools.description:
Estimate the monthly cost of a database instance BEFORE creating it using the SelfHost pricing API.
Call this to present accurate cost to the user for approval before calling create_instance.

Returns an itemized breakdown of compute, storage and add-ons. Prices are ALL-IN: the
platform margin is folded into each line rather than billed separately, matching the
console and the website - so quote these numbers to the user as-is and never add a
platform fee on top.

Pass type_of_dbms whenever you know the engine. ClickHouse prices differently: with
replica_count=1 the platform provisions a third, keeper-only node (t4g.small + 20 GB) to hold
the Raft quorum, and this tool only includes it when it knows the engine. Leave the engine
out for a ClickHouse cluster and the estimate understates the real bill.

CLICKHOUSE ESTIMATES RUN LOW EVEN WITH THE ENGINE PASSED, and the keeper node is not the
reason. The estimate endpoint applies ONE flat platform margin to every engine, while
billing applies the real per-engine margin - and ClickHouse's is higher than the flat one.
So a ClickHouse estimate lands roughly 10% below what the instance will actually bill. Present
it as an approximate floor for ClickHouse, not the figure the user will be charged. Every
other AWS engine estimates at its true margin and needs no such caveat.

THIS IS AWS ONLY. It cannot price a PaaS project server - those are Hetzner machines on a
different margin entirely. Use `list_server_types`, which returns real per-location prices.

iops.description: Provisioned IOPS (for gp3/io1/io2). Defaults to storage type baseline if omitted.

throughput_mbps.description: Throughput in MB/s (for gp3). Defaults to storage type baseline if omitted.

type_of_dbms.description: Engine being priced. Only changes the maths for clickhouse with replica_count=1, where the billed Keeper node is added to the estimate.

tools.name: create_instance
tools.description:
Create a new database instance on AWS. This is the core AWS provisioning tool.

RECOMMENDED FLOW (follow this before calling create_instance):
1. Ask the user: host on SelfHost's cloud (platform-managed) or their own AWS account (BYOC)?
2. Call list_credentials - filter results by cloud_provider "aws" AND status "active".
   - Platform-managed: pick credential where is_platform_managed=true
   - BYOC: pick credential where is_platform_managed=false. If none exist, user must add_credential first.
3. If BYOC: call list_vpcs with the credential's id and chosen region - only present VPCs from the "public" group. vpc_id is REQUIRED for BYOC.
4. If platform-managed: vpc_id is NOT needed (skip VPC selection entirely).
5. Call estimate_instance_cost to show the user the estimated monthly cost before deploying.
6. Only call create_instance after the user confirms the cost is acceptable.

IMPORTANT:
- The password in the response is shown ONCE and can never be retrieved again. Save it immediately.
- public_access is always true (private access not yet supported).
- Storage IOPS/throughput requirements depend on storage type:
  gp3: iops required (3000-80000), throughput required (125-1000 MB/s)
  io1/io2: iops required (100+), throughput NOT used
  gp2/st1/sc1: iops and throughput NOT used

CLICKHOUSE SPECIFICS (they differ from the other engines - read before creating one):
- Minimum 4 GiB RAM. Smaller instance types are rejected; find eligible sizes with
  get_instance_types_for_region using min_memory=4.
- Replication is a Keeper/Raft quorum, not streaming replication, so multi_az REQUIRES
  replica_count >= 1 and the count changes the node topology:
    replica_count=1 → primary + 1 replica + a dedicated Keeper node (t4g.small, 20 GB)
                      that holds the quorum. That third node is billed - price it with
                      estimate_instance_cost using type_of_dbms="clickhouse".
    replica_count=2+ → primary + N replicas, quorum embedded on the data nodes, no extra node.
  2 is the recommended default and is what gets used if you enable multi_az without a count.
- Connect over HTTP on 8123 (native TCP on 9000) as user `admin`. Multi-AZ clusters
  expose the distributed cluster `selfhost_cluster`.
- Use 8123 as the port on allowed_cidr_ranges entries, not 5432/3306.
- Versions: 24.3, 24.8, 25.1, 26.5 (defaults to the 24.8 LTS).

ENGINE-SPECIFIC FOLLOW-UPS (route to the right tools per engine after creating):
- Connection pooling: PgBouncer for postgres, ProxySQL for mysql, CHProxy for clickhouse, none for redis.
- Performance tuning: the pg-config tools for postgres, the mysql-config tools for mysql; none for redis or clickhouse.
- PITR applies to postgres and mysql only - not redis, not clickhouse.
- database-users applies to postgres, mysql and clickhouse - not redis.
- postgresql_config and the two extension flags are postgres-only.
- db_version can be upgraded in place on clickhouse only (upgrade_clickhouse_version).

POSTGRES EXTENSIONS (neither is a separate engine - both are postgres + a flag):
- timescaledb_enabled → TimescaleDB (hypertables, continuous aggregates, compression) for
  time-series workloads. Installing it at create costs nothing extra; enabling it later
  restarts PostgreSQL once (enable_timescaledb).
- vector_enabled → pgvector (the `vector` type + similarity search) for embeddings.
- Both can be on at once here, and both are ENABLE-ONLY - the backend refuses to turn
  either off afterwards, so ask the user before setting them.

tools.name: list_instances
tools.description:
List all database instances for an organization, grouped by `group_id` (master + replicas).

POLL `ready`, NOT `status`. Each instance carries a server-computed `ready` boolean, a `ha_ready` for the group, and a `readiness_detail` hash explaining a false. That exists precisely so a caller stops guessing across `status`, `internal_status`, `provisioning_state` and replica health - a `running` instance is NOT necessarily usable. Answer "is my database up?" from `ready`.

`ha_ready` is the one to check before telling a user their cluster is highly available: it is true only when the master is ready AND every live replica's replication link is healthy, so it goes false on a quietly degraded cluster whose master still looks fine.

`deprecated_at` on an instance means its machine type is being retired. It keeps working, but flag it - a user planning capacity should know before the deadline rather than after.

tools.name: get_instance
tools.description:
Get detailed information about a specific database instance, including its latest metrics.

READINESS IS ONE FIELD. `ready` is computed server-side and is the field to trust: for a master or single node it means running, provisioning complete, no error, and the agent healthy; for a replica it means running, complete, and the replication LINK healthy (a small lag is fine - only a broken link blocks readiness). `readiness_detail` says which of those failed. Do not reassemble this from `status` and `internal_status`; a `running` instance can be unusable.

`ha_ready` covers the whole group: master ready and every alive HA replica link-healthy.

If an instance has been provisioning for more than about 15 minutes it is considered STUCK rather than slow - say so instead of advising the user to keep waiting.

`deprecated_at`, when set, marks the machine type as scheduled for retirement. Worth surfacing unprompted.

instance_id.description: AWS EC2 instance ID (alternative to pid)

snapshot_id.description: Snapshot ID (to get original instance context for restore)

tools.name: get_instance_metrics
tools.description:
Read historical metrics for managed database instances - the same agent-heartbeat series the console graphs.

Use this to answer "how is my database doing?", to size a change before making it, or to sanity-check an alert rule (a rule on a metric that never appears here will never fire).

Returns a per-instance, per-metric summary (latest / min / max / avg + sample count) by default. Set raw=true only when you genuinely need every sample - a busy instance produces hundreds of frames per day and they will flood the context.

Metric sets (same names alert rules use):
- system: cpu_percent, memory_percent, disk_usage_percent, load_avg_1/5/15, swap_usage_percent, cpu_io_wait_percent
- network: recv_bytes_per_sec, sent_bytes_per_sec
- storage: disk_used_percent, disk_free_bytes, inodes_used_percent, read/write_io_per_second, ... reported PER MOUNT POINT and keyed `storage[/mount]` in the summary. Read the engine's data volume (e.g. `storage[/selfhostdev/postgresql]`), not `storage[/]` or `storage[/boot]` - a full /boot says nothing about database capacity.
- <engine>.database: postgresql.database | mysql.database | redis.database | clickhouse.database - the engine's own counters. `create_alert_rule` carries the complete per-engine allow-list; these are the same names.
- pgbouncer.stats appears once pooling is enabled. It is READABLE here but NOT alertable - the alert-rule catalog has no such metric_type, so a rule on it is rejected.

On a replicated instance `active_replica_count` is the one to watch for a quietly-degraded cluster: it drops without the instance's own status changing. Ratio metrics (`cache_hit_ratio`, `innodb_buffer_pool_hit_ratio`, `mark_cache_hit_ratio`) are already on a 0-100 scale - do not multiply them by 100.

An empty result usually means the agent has not reported in that window (a stopped instance, or one still provisioning), not that the instance is idle.

instance_pid.description: Limit to one instance (awsinst_...). Omit for every instance in the org.

start_date.description: Inclusive start date, YYYY-MM-DD (default: yesterday). The window covers whole days.

metric_type.description: Only return this metric set. Cheaper than filtering client-side.

raw.description: Return every heartbeat frame instead of the summary. Verbose - use a narrow window and a single instance.

tools.name: upgrade_clickhouse_version
tools.description:
Upgrade a ClickHouse instance to a newer version in place (ClickHouse is the only engine with an in-place version upgrade - the backend rejects db_version changes on every other engine).

Rules the backend enforces:
- One version at a time, along the supported ladder: 24.3 → 24.8 → 25.1 → 26.5. Skipping a
  step is rejected with the next allowed version named in the error.
- The instance must have a registered agent.
- Requesting the version it already runs is a no-op success.

The upgrade restarts clickhouse-server on the node, so expect a brief interruption. Take a
snapshot first (create_snapshot) - that is the rollback path if the upgrade goes wrong.

db_version.description: Target ClickHouse version - must be exactly one step above the current one

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user to confirm, and recommend a snapshot first.

tools.name: stop_instance
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: Stop one or more running database instances. Databases become unavailable. A replica cannot be stopped on its own - stop the master and the group goes with it.

STOPPING DOES NOT STOP THE BILL, and this is the most common wrong assumption to correct. Compute stops accruing, but everything that still physically exists keeps being charged: the EBS volumes, snapshots, and S3-backed storage including PITR WAL. A stopped instance is cheaper, not free. If the user's goal is to stop paying, the answer is `delete_instance` (and deleting snapshots separately) - say so rather than letting them believe a stop achieved it.

A final charge is issued at the moment of the stop, closing the window since the last billing run, so the next invoice includes usage right up to the transition.

You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user for explicit confirmation before setting this.

tools.name: start_instance
tools.description:
Start one or more stopped database instances. A replica cannot be started on its own.

Compute resumes billing from the moment it starts. If the wallet is empty this can fail on the balance gate - check `get_wallet_balance` first when a start is refused rather than retrying.

tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: Delete one or more database instances. This action is irreversible.
Delete protection must be disabled first. Master deletion must include all replicas.

A final charge is issued at deletion for usage since the last billing run, so a small charge after deleting is correct, not a bug.

WHAT SURVIVES THE DELETE AND KEEPS BILLING: snapshots and other backup storage are separate resources and are NOT removed with the instance. If the user is deleting in order to stop paying, check `list_snapshots` and `list_backups` too - otherwise they will delete the database and keep the storage bill.

You MUST set confirm=true to proceed. Before calling this tool, always ask the user to confirm they want to delete these specific instances.

tools.name: list_backups
tools.description:
List backups for an organization. Triggers a sync with AWS to refresh snapshot sizes.

Covers both families - read `backup_type` on each row to tell them apart (`aws_backup_job` = disk snapshot, `clickhouse_native` = ClickHouse data backup). A data-backup row additionally carries `options.backup_name`, `options.s3_bucket`, `options.scheduled` (true when a schedule took it), `options.backup_policy_pid`, a measured `size_bytes`, `error_message` on failure, and `options.last_restore` (`in_progress` | `completed` | `failed`) once it has been restored from.

There is no single-backup GET: to follow a run or a restore to completion, call this again. A backup's own `status` stays `completed` whatever a later restore does - only `options.last_restore` moves.

tools.name: create_backup
tools.description:
Take a backup of a database instance now. Cannot back up a replica.

TWO TYPES, pick the one that matches what the user asked for:
- `aws_backup_job` - a DISK SNAPSHOT via AWS Backup. Any engine. Needs `options: {backup_vault_name, backup_plan_id}`. Restored by creating a new instance from the resulting `snapshot_id`, not by `restore_backup`.
- `clickhouse_native` - a DATA BACKUP: `BACKUP ALL` of every database, streamed to a dedicated offsite S3 bucket. ClickHouse DATA nodes only (a keeper-only node holds no table data). No `options` required - the backend resolves and provisions the bucket. This is the only type `restore_backup` accepts.

`s3_file_backup` was removed: the backend now 422s it and tells you to use `clickhouse_native`. Do not try it.

EXPECT THESE REFUSALS on `clickhouse_native`, all 422 and all worth explaining rather than retrying blindly: the instance is not running; a restore is in progress; a backup is already in flight (one per instance, a hard lock). A 503 means the backup bucket could not be provisioned - that one IS retryable and leaves no doomed record.

Returns the run in `in_progress`. Poll `list_backups` for the terminal state.

COSTS MONEY: snapshot storage is metered per GB-month against your credit wallet (SKU `ebs_snapshot_storage`; see `list_skus` for the rate) and keeps billing until the snapshot is deleted. A 402 here means the wallet is empty or no payment method is linked - top up with `create_topup` / `link_billing_payment_method`.

tools.name: restore_backup
tools.description:
Restore a ClickHouse DATA backup (`clickhouse_native`) back into a running ClickHouse instance. This is the only restore path here - a DISK SNAPSHOT is not restored with this tool, you create a new instance from its `snapshot_id` instead.

THE RESTORE IS ADDITIVE. It MERGES the backup's tables into the target and never drops anything already there. It is not "roll back to this point": a row written after the backup was taken survives the restore. Say that to the user before running it, because "restore" usually means the opposite.

By default it restores into the instance the backup came from. Pass `target_instance_id` to restore into a DIFFERENT running ClickHouse data node - that is how you clone a dataset between instances. Pass `databases` to narrow the scope; names must be plain identifiers or the backend 422s.

While it runs the TARGET instance sits in status `restoring` (cleared on success and on failure alike). Refusals, all 422: the backup is not `clickhouse_native`, is deleted, or is not `completed`; it has no offsite S3 copy so there is nothing to read; the target is not ClickHouse, is not running, or is already restoring; or a backup is in flight on the target (running BACKUP ALL and RESTORE ALL together would capture a dataset mid-mutation and mark it completed).

Follow it with `list_backups` and read `options.last_restore` - the backup's own `status` stays `completed` regardless of how the restore ends.

target_instance_id.description: Restore into this instance instead of the one the backup was taken from. Must be a RUNNING ClickHouse data node.

databases.description: Restore only these databases. Plain identifiers only. Omit to restore everything in the backup.

confirm.description: Must be true. Confirm the user understands the restore MERGES into the target and does not roll it back.

tools.name: delete_backup
tools.description: DESTRUCTIVE: Delete a backup. Removes the AWS snapshot if present and soft-deletes the backup record. This cannot be undone. You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user for explicit confirmation before setting this.

tools.name: list_backup_policies
tools.description:
List backup schedules for an organization. Optionally filter by instance.

TWO KINDS come back in the same list and you must read `details.policy_type` to tell them apart:
- absent / anything else = a DLM DISK-SNAPSHOT policy (block-level EBS snapshots, any engine).
- `clickhouse_native` = a ClickHouse DATA-BACKUP schedule (`BACKUP ALL` to offsite S3).

An instance can have BOTH at once, and they are independent. Do not present a native row as the instance's snapshot policy or vice versa - the console had a bug where one shadowed the other and users read the wrong retention.

Each row carries `schedule_interval` + `schedule_unit` + `retain_rule_count` and a `state` of `ENABLED` or `DISABLED` (that is the paused flag).

tools.name: create_backup_policy
tools.description:
Create a DLM policy for automated DISK SNAPSHOTS (block-level EBS). Any engine.

For a ClickHouse DATA-BACKUP schedule use `create_data_backup_schedule` instead - it is a different resource with different required fields, and this tool cannot make one.

If the instance is ClickHouse, note a temporary backend coupling: saving the disk-snapshot policy currently also rewrites and re-enables the instance's data-backup schedule. Warn the user if they have both.

COSTS MONEY: snapshot storage is metered per GB-month against your credit wallet (SKU `ebs_snapshot_storage`; see `list_skus` for the rate) and keeps billing until the snapshot is deleted. A 402 here means the wallet is empty or no payment method is linked - top up with `create_topup` / `link_billing_payment_method`. A schedule multiplies that: the policy holds `retain_rule_count` snapshots per volume at once, so the standing cost is roughly retention x volume size.

tools.name: create_data_backup_schedule
tools.description:
Create a recurring ClickHouse DATA-BACKUP schedule: a `BACKUP ALL` of every database, streamed to a dedicated offsite S3 bucket, on a cadence you set. ClickHouse only. This is the scheduled counterpart of `create_backup` with `backup_type: "clickhouse_native"`.

Not the same thing as `create_backup_policy`, which schedules block-level DISK SNAPSHOTS. An instance can carry one of each.

ONE PER INSTANCE. A second create returns 422 naming the existing schedule - update or delete that one instead.

Retention is `retain_rule_count` runs kept, pruned oldest-first. Send integers, never numeric strings: the backend rejects a non-integer, and the reason it is strict is that a string would cast to 0 and 0 means "every run" for the interval and "never prune" for the retention.

A 503 means the offsite bucket could not be provisioned. That is retryable and leaves nothing behind.

COSTS MONEY: snapshot storage is metered per GB-month against your credit wallet (SKU `ebs_snapshot_storage`; see `list_skus` for the rate) and keeps billing until the snapshot is deleted. A 402 here means the wallet is empty or no payment method is linked - top up with `create_topup` / `link_billing_payment_method`. Here the metered cost is S3 storage for the retained backups, not EBS.

cloud_instance_pid.description: The ClickHouse instance to back up. Must be a data node - a keeper-only node holds no table data.

schedule_interval.description: How often, as a positive integer paired with schedule_unit (e.g. 1 + DAYS = daily)

retain_rule_count.description: How many completed backups to keep. Older ones are pruned.

region.description: Defaults to the instance's own region - normally omit this

tools.name: update_backup_policy
tools.description:
Update a backup schedule. Works on BOTH kinds - the backend routes on the policy's own type, so pass the pid and the fields you want changed.

PAUSE AND RESUME is `state`: `DISABLED` pauses the schedule and KEEPS everything it has already taken; `ENABLED` resumes it. Prefer this over deleting whenever the user says "stop backups for now" - deleting a data-backup schedule destroys its runs (see `delete_backup_policy`).

On a ClickHouse DATA-BACKUP schedule (`details.policy_type == "clickhouse_native"`) only `state`, `schedule_interval`, `schedule_unit` and `retain_rule_count` apply; the DLM-only fields are ignored. Send integers, not numeric strings, or the backend 422s.

On a DISK-SNAPSHOT (DLM) policy, shortening retention is checked against the object-storage restore window and is refused with a 422 if the retained snapshots would outlive it.

state.description: DISABLED pauses the schedule and keeps existing backups; ENABLED resumes it

tools.name: delete_backup_policy
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: Delete a backup schedule. Works on both kinds, and WHAT IT DESTROYS DIFFERS:

- DISK-SNAPSHOT (DLM) policy: removes the policy from AWS and stops future snapshots. Snapshots already taken survive.
- ClickHouse DATA-BACKUP schedule (`details.policy_type == "clickhouse_native"`): also DELETES every backup that schedule took - the S3 folders, the rows, and the dedicated bucket once nothing else references it. Manual backups of the same instance are untouched. This is a deliberate backend decision, not a bug.

So on a data-backup schedule this is not "stop backing up", it is "stop backing up AND throw away the scheduled history". If the user only wants to stop, call `update_backup_policy` with `state: "DISABLED"` instead - that pauses and keeps everything. OFFER THAT FIRST.

Either way, if this was the last active policy on the instance, `backup_enabled` is turned off.

You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user for explicit confirmation before setting this.

tools.description:
Create an alert rule for monitoring. Set cloud_instance_pid to target a specific instance, or omit for an org-wide rule.

THE METRIC ALLOW-LIST. `metric_name` must appear under the `metric_type` you pass or the rule is rejected:

- system: cpu_percent, cpu_io_wait_percent, memory_percent, swap_usage_percent, disk_usage_percent, load_avg_1, load_avg_5, load_avg_15
- network: recv_bytes_per_sec, sent_bytes_per_sec
- storage: disk_free_bytes, disk_free_percent, disk_total_bytes, disk_used_bytes, disk_used_percent, inodes_free, inodes_total, inodes_used, inodes_used_percent, read_bytes_per_second, read_io_per_second, read_utilization_percent, read_write_bytes_per_second, total_utilization_percent, write_bytes_per_second, write_io_per_second, write_utilization_percent
- postgresql.database: blocks_read_per_second, cache_hit_ratio, committed_tx_per_second, connections_total, max_connections, replication_lag_seconds, active_replica_count, transactions_per_second, timescaledb_hypertable_count, timescaledb_chunk_count, timescaledb_compressed_chunk_count, timescaledb_compression_ratio, timescaledb_total_size_bytes
- mysql.database: connections_total, max_connections, connections_aborted, threads_running, queries_per_second, slow_queries_per_second, replication_lag_seconds, active_replica_count, innodb_buffer_pool_hit_ratio, innodb_row_lock_waits_per_second, tmp_disk_tables_per_second, select_full_scans_per_second
- redis.database: used_memory, connected_clients, evicted_keys, expired_keys, keyspace_hits, keyspace_misses, instantaneous_ops_per_sec, rdb_changes_since_last_save, rdb_last_save_time, replication_lag_seconds, connected_slaves, blocked_clients
- clickhouse.database: query_count, queries_per_second, select_queries_per_second, insert_queries_per_second, failed_queries_per_second, inserted_rows_per_second, selected_rows_per_second, memory_usage, background_merges_count, replication_delay, replication_lag_seconds, active_replica_count, disk_used_bytes, connections_count, connections_total, broken_parts_count, mark_cache_hit_ratio, parts_active, keeper_connected, total_replicas, active_replicas, queue_size, future_parts, is_session_expired, lost_replicas, noquorum_detached_parts

Match metric_type to the instance's ENGINE. A rule using postgresql.database metrics never fires on a ClickHouse instance - it is accepted and then silently never evaluates, which is worse than an error, so check the engine with `get_instance` first if you are unsure.

Metrics that exist but never arrive are the other silent failure. The five `timescaledb_*` names are absent from heartbeats until TimescaleDB is actually installed, and `active_replica_count` only means something on a replicated instance. A rule on a metric the instance does not report does not error - it just never fires. `get_instance_metrics` shows what an instance is really sending; if a name is missing there, a rule on it is dead.

Two engine-specific traps worth knowing:
- ClickHouse reports replication health as `replication_delay` (seconds behind the quorum). `replication_lag_seconds` also exists but `replication_delay` is the one the platform's own sync logic reads.
- Ratio metrics are already percentages on the 0-100 scale - `cache_hit_ratio`, `innodb_buffer_pool_hit_ratio` and `mark_cache_hit_ratio` alike. Set a threshold like 95, not 0.95. (`timescaledb_compression_ratio` is the exception: it is a multiplier, so 3.5 means 3.5x.) Redis has no ready-made ratio - compute it from `keyspace_hits` and `keyspace_misses`.

`storage` rules REQUIRE `mount_point`, and it must name a real mount on the instance (`/`, `/boot`, or the engine's data volume - they are reported separately and a rule on the wrong one watches the wrong disk).

tools.name: list_database_users
tools.description:
List DBMS-level users on an instance. Returns each user's id, username, role, status (`active` | `pending` | `deleting` | `failed`), target database, connection limit, password expiry metadata and `password_rotation_enabled`. Postgres, MySQL and ClickHouse (not Redis).

Read `password_rotation_enabled` alongside the expiry when a user asks about credentials: `false` means the credential will be LOCKED at expiry (warned by email first), `true` means it will be silently rotated and a webhook fired. A credential nearing expiry with the wrong setting for how it is consumed is the failure worth flagging without being asked.

A `failed` user whose error mentions enforcement sync means a lock half-applied; `rotate_database_user_password` recovers it.

tools.name: create_database_user
tools.description:
Create a DBMS-level user on an instance. Postgres, MySQL and ClickHouse - NOT supported for Redis (Redis uses a single shared requirepass; the backend returns "Database user management not supported for redis"). Username 1-31 chars, letters/digits/underscores only. Password 8-128 printable chars. Role determines DB privileges: read_only (SELECT), read_write (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), admin (broader DDL). Target database scopes the grant to one DB; leave empty for cluster-level access.

PASSWORD LIFETIME: every user's password expires after 90 days, and what happens then depends on `password_rotation_enabled`:

- `false` (THE DEFAULT) - the user gets reminder emails at 14, 3 and 1 days out. At expiry the credential is ROTATED TO A PASSWORD NOBODY IS TOLD and locked, so it stops working until someone calls `rotate_database_user_password`. Right for a human who logs in and can act on a warning; wrong for an app, because the app just breaks.
- `true` - no emails and no lock. At expiry the password rotates automatically and a `database_user.password_rotated` webhook fires so the consumer can fetch the new credential (the webhook payload never carries the password itself). Right for tooling that can refetch on that signal.

The default is `false` deliberately: silent rotation breaks credentials baked into an application, which is what users complained about. So `true` is only the better choice if something is actually listening for that webhook and can refetch. If a password is hardcoded anywhere, `true` will break it silently at the 90-day mark instead of warning first - ASK which situation this user is in rather than guessing.

The instance must be `running` or `provisioned`, and the username must be free.

target_database.description: Specific DB to grant on; omit for cluster-wide

connection_limit.description: Max concurrent connections for this user (default unlimited)

password_expiry_days.description: Days until the password expires; omit for no expiry

password_rotation_enabled.description: false (default) = warn by email, then lock the credential at expiry. true = rotate silently at expiry and fire a `database_user.password_rotated` webhook instead. Only pick true if something is listening for that webhook - it will break a hardcoded password with no warning.

tools.name: update_database_user
tools.description:
Update a database user - change role, connection limit, password expiry, or the expiry BEHAVIOUR. Username and target database are immutable (delete + recreate to change them). Postgres, MySQL and ClickHouse (not Redis).

The password itself is not changed here: use `rotate_database_user_password` for that (it reveals the new password once).

Switching `password_rotation_enabled` is the fix for a credential heading for the wrong ending. Set it `true` when an app consumes the credential and can refetch on the `database_user.password_rotated` webhook, so expiry rotates instead of locking. Set it `false` when a person uses the credential and should be warned by email rather than have it change under them.

A user that has ALREADY been locked by an expiry is not recovered by flipping this - it stays locked until `rotate_database_user_password` runs.

password_expiry_days.description: 0 removes expiry; otherwise sets a new countdown from now

password_rotation_enabled.description: true = auto-rotate at expiry and fire the `database_user.password_rotated` webhook. false = email warnings, then lock the credential at expiry.

tools.description: Soft-delete a database user. Existing connections opened by this user are terminated. The record is preserved for audit - contact support to recover. Postgres, MySQL and ClickHouse (not Redis).

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Existing connections will be dropped.

tools.name: rotate_database_user_password
tools.description: Rotate the password for a database user. The new password is generated server-side and returned ONCE in the response. SECURITY: save it immediately - there is no way to retrieve it later. Existing connections using the old password are terminated. Postgres, MySQL and ClickHouse (not Redis).

confirm.description: Must be true. Old password is invalidated immediately; apps and scripts must pick up the new value.

tools.name: scale_instance
tools.description:
Manual one-off resize of an instance - change instance type, volume type, size, IOPS, throughput. Only fields you pass are sent (PATCH-style). Response includes `scaling_event_id` you can poll on the instance status (`resizing` / `modifying_storage` → terminal state). Storage must grow, not shrink.

STORAGE CASCADES: growing a data node's volume also expands every live data peer in its cluster to match, and storage bills per node - so on a multi-node cluster the cost of `new_size_gb` is multiplied by the number of data nodes. Tell the user before scaling a clustered instance. (Unlike an auto-scale rule, a manual scale takes an absolute size and ignores any cluster_max_storage_gb ceiling.)

new_size_gb.description: New EBS size; must be ≥ current

new_iops.description: Only valid for gp3/io1/io2 volume types

tools.name: list_scaling_policies
tools.description:
List scaling policies, optionally filtered to one instance. Covers start/stop schedules, auto-scaling rules and cluster tier triggers; each row carries `cloud_instance_pid` so you can tell which instance it belongs to.

TELLING THE THREE APART matters, because they behave nothing alike:
- `cloud_instance_pid` set, `group_id` empty - an ordinary single-instance rule.
- `group_id` set with `scaling_action: resize_instance` - a CLUSTER TIER trigger. It moves the whole group along a capacity ladder and its thresholds are the `cpu_*`/`memory_*` pair plus `window_minutes`, not `metric_name`/`threshold`. Its bounds live on the group's capacity config (`get_capacity_config`), so this row alone does not tell you how far the group can move. Tier triggers come in pairs - one `scale_up`, one `scale_down` - and a group with only an up policy will grow and never shrink, which is worth pointing out.
- Filtering by instance will NOT return a group's tier policies, since they have no instance target. Use `get_capacity_config` for those.

An `expand_storage` policy whose `details` still has `new_size_gb` (instead of `cluster_max_storage_gb`) predates the cluster-cascade contract: it is outdated, cannot be edited or disabled (every save 422s), and must be deleted and recreated. Flag those to the user rather than trying to patch them.

organization_id.description: Org PID; defaults to active org. Used as `organization_pid` on the wire.

tools.name: create_scaling_policy
tools.description:
Create a scaling policy. Use this for both auto-start/stop schedules and reactive/scheduled auto-scaling rules. Shape depends on action + trigger:

• start/stop schedules → schedule_type=scheduled + scheduled_start_time OR scheduled_stop_time (HH:MM UTC) + days_of_week. These are the only policies that may target MANY instances (cloud_instance_pids).
• reactive auto-scale  → schedule_type=reactive + metric_name + comparison_operator + threshold + duration_minutes + cooldown_minutes
• scheduled auto-scale → schedule_type=scheduled + cron_expression (5-field) + optional start_time/end_time (ISO 8601). The reactive fields are still required by the backend; neutral defaults are injected for you (manual_trigger / 85 / '>' / 1m / 0 cooldown) and ignored at fire time.

Action-specific `details` (required on every non-start/stop policy):
• resize_instance → { target_instance_type }
• add_replica     → { max_replicas }
• expand_storage  → { cluster_max_storage_gb }

STORAGE AUTO-SCALE (expand_storage) - read before writing one:
- Growth is a DOUBLING on each fire, clamped to cluster_max_storage_gb and the volume type's own max: target = min(current x 2, cluster_max, type_max). There is no absolute-size or step option; details.new_size_gb and details.growth_step_gb are rejected (422). For a one-off absolute resize use `scale_instance`.
- cluster_max_storage_gb must EXCEED the volume's current size.
- threshold must be between 40 and 85, and the operator must be '>' or '>=' (disk metrics: disk_used_percent / disk_usage_percent).
- The rule may only attach to a DATA, non-replica node (ClickHouse keeper-only nodes are not data nodes).
- Expansion CASCADES: when the volume commits, every live data peer in the cluster is expanded to match, and storage bills per node. Warn the user about the multiplied cost on a multi-node cluster.

TIER POLICIES (whole-cluster ladder scaling) are a FOURTH shape and none of the above applies to them. A policy is a tier policy when `scaling_action` is `resize_instance` AND `group_id` is set:
- Required: `group_id`, `target_class`, `direction` (`scale_up` or `scale_down`), and `window_minutes`.
- Thresholds are the direction's CPU **and** memory pair - `cpu_up_threshold` + `memory_up_threshold` for up, `cpu_down_threshold` + `memory_down_threshold` for down. NOT `metric_name` / `threshold` / `comparison_operator`, which are ignored.
- `schedule_type` is FORBIDDEN (422). Tier scaling is reactive only.
- `details.target_instance_type` is NOT used - the ladder decides the next size.
- ONE POLICY PER DIRECTION. Scaling up and scaling down are two separate rules against the same group.
- An enabled capacity config for (`group_id`, `target_class`) must ALREADY EXIST or this is refused. Create it with `create_capacity_config` first.
- HYSTERESIS IS ENFORCED across the pair: a scale_down threshold must be strictly below its scale_up sibling, on both CPU and memory. Equal values are rejected, because they would let the cluster oscillate.
- Server defaults if omitted: 80/80 up, 20/20 down, `window_minutes` 10 up and 360 down, cooldown 30. The long scale-down window is intentional - a quiet afternoon should not shrink a production cluster.
- Use this instead of a plain `resize_instance` rule for any clustered engine: a single-node switchover fired at a multi-node cluster desyncs its tier state.

organization_id.description: Org PID; defaults to active org. Wire field: organization_pid

cloud_instance_pid.description: Target instance PID. Required for every action except bulk start/stop schedules, which may use cloud_instance_pids instead.

cloud_instance_pids.description: Multiple target instances - ONLY valid for start_instance / stop_instance schedules. The backend rejects it for expand_storage / resize_instance / add_replica.

metric_name.description: Metric to watch. Disk fill reports as disk_used_percent (also accepted: disk_usage_percent).

threshold.description: 0-100 for percentage metrics. expand_storage is restricted to 40-85.

timezone.description: Default UTC; BE supports UTC | EST | PST | GMT | CET

group_id.description: TIER POLICY: the instance group to scale as a whole. Setting this with scaling_action `resize_instance` makes this a tier policy, not a single-instance resize. Requires an enabled capacity config for (group_id, target_class).

target_class.description: TIER POLICY: which plane this trigger governs. `data` is the normal choice; `non_data` is ClickHouse keepers.

direction.description: TIER POLICY: required. One policy per direction - up and down are separate rules, not one rule with two thresholds.

cpu_up_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_up): CPU percent that must be exceeded. Defaults to 80.

memory_up_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_up): memory percent that must be exceeded. Defaults to 80. Both CPU and memory apply.

cpu_down_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_down): CPU percent to fall below. Defaults to 20. Must be strictly BELOW the sibling scale_up threshold.

memory_down_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_down): memory percent to fall below. Defaults to 20. Must be strictly BELOW the sibling scale_up threshold.

window_minutes.description: TIER POLICY: how long the condition must hold. Defaults to 10 for scale_up, 360 for scale_down - the asymmetry is deliberate, so a lull does not shrink a cluster.

details.description: Action-specific payload: { target_instance_type } | { cluster_max_storage_gb } | { max_replicas }. Required for every action except start_instance / stop_instance.

tools.name: update_scaling_policy
tools.description:
Update an existing scaling policy. Only the fields you pass are changed - but note the backend re-validates the WHOLE policy, so a rule written under the old storage contract cannot be edited.

LEGACY expand_storage RULES: policies still carrying details.new_size_gb are outdated and every save 422s. There is no in-place migration - delete the rule and create a fresh one with details.cluster_max_storage_gb. Disabling one also fails; only `delete_scaling_policy` works.

Pass scaling_action when you know it so the storage-specific rules (40-85 threshold band, '>' / '>=' only, doubling ceiling) can be checked before the request goes out.

direction.description: TIER POLICY only. Changing direction rewrites which threshold pair applies - normally leave alone.

cpu_up_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_up). Must stay above the sibling scale_down value.

memory_up_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_up). Must stay above the sibling scale_down value.

cpu_down_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_down). Must stay below the sibling scale_up value.

memory_down_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_down). Must stay below the sibling scale_up value.

window_minutes.description: TIER POLICY: how long the condition must hold before firing.

scaling_action.description: The policy's action, from `list_scaling_policies`. Not sent as a change - used to validate the fields below against the right rules.

details.description: Replacement action payload: { target_instance_type } | { cluster_max_storage_gb } | { max_replicas }.

tools.name: delete_scaling_policy
tools.description: Delete a scaling policy. The associated instance is unaffected - only the schedule / rule is removed.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed.

tools.name: get_pitr
tools.description: Get PITR config + restore window for an instance. Returns null when PITR has never been configured. Response includes s3_bucket, retention_days, oldest_restore_point, latest_restore_point, last_base_backup_at, and error_message when status=error.

tools.name: enable_pitr
tools.description: Enable PITR on a Postgres or MySQL instance - streams the transaction log to S3 continuously and takes nightly base backups. Postgres archives WAL (via wal-g); MySQL archives binlog with ~1 minute restore granularity. Not available for Redis or ClickHouse. The S3 bucket must exist in the same region; the instance role needs s3:PutObject / GetObject / ListBucket. Status transitions: configuring → enabled (or error).

s3_bucket.description: S3 bucket name (must exist in same region)

retention_days.description: Days of WAL to keep (default 7, range 1-35). Longer = larger S3 bill.

tools.name: configure_pitr
tools.description: Toggle an existing PITR config between `enabled` (resume WAL archiving) and `disabled` (pause). The bucket and retention are preserved either way. Use `enable_pitr` for first-time setup, not this.

status.description: Target state - enabled resumes WAL, disabled pauses it

tools.name: retry_pitr
tools.description: Retry PITR setup after an `error` state. Common error causes: missing IAM permissions on the bucket, wrong bucket region, or archiver setup failure (wal-g on Postgres, binlog streaming on MySQL). Fix the underlying issue first, then retry.

tools.name: trigger_pitr_base_backup
tools.description: Trigger a one-off base backup now. Runs in the background (Postgres uses `wal-g backup-push`; MySQL takes a full base backup) - your instance keeps serving traffic. Useful before risky migrations or to seed the restore window after a fresh enable. Postgres and MySQL only.

tools.name: list_pitr_base_backups
tools.description: List historical base backups for an instance. Each row carries status (pending | running | completed | failed), started_at, completed_at, and error_message when failed.

tools.name: restore_pitr
tools.description: Restore an instance to a point in time. Creates a NEW instance of the same engine (Postgres or MySQL) recovered to `target_time` - the source instance is untouched. `target_time` must fall within the source instance's [oldest_restore_point, latest_restore_point] window (see `get_pitr`). `name` is the new instance name; must start with a letter and use letters/digits/hyphens only.

name.description: Name for the new restored instance

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. A new instance will be provisioned (provider charges apply).

tools.name: get_wallet_balance
tools.description:
Get the organization's prepaid credit-wallet balance. Returns `balance_cents` + `balance_formatted`, currency, `payment_channel_state` (`unlinked` | `linking` | `chargeable`), `hourly_burn_rate_cents` (current spend rate), `estimated_hours_remaining` (runway), `expiring_soon`, and the linked card. Credit is consumed hourly while resources run; at $0 resources are stopped until topped up. There are no plans or tiers.

CHECK `expiring_soon` AND SAY SO UNPROMPTED. Some credit has an expiry date, so a healthy-looking balance can be about to shrink without anything being spent. A runway computed from `balance_cents` alone overstates it in that case. If `expiring_soon` is non-empty, tell the user what expires and when alongside the balance - it is the one thing here they cannot infer from the number they already see.

`estimated_hours_remaining` is balance divided by the CURRENT burn rate, so it assumes today's resources keep running unchanged. It is not a forecast: provisioning anything new shortens it immediately, and it is null when nothing is running.

tools.name: list_skus
tools.description: List the priced resource catalog (SKUs). Each SKU has resource_type, hourly_rate_cents + hourly_rate_formatted, and currency. Use this to estimate how long a top-up will last for a given resource.

tools.name: list_credit_ledger
tools.description: List credit-wallet ledger entries (most recent first). entry_type is `topup` (credit added), `free_credit` (welcome grant - has expires_at), or `usage_charge` (hourly deduction, negative). amount_cents is signed; remaining_cents shows how much of a positive lot is left.

tools.name: list_wallet_transactions
tools.description: List per-resource hourly billing transactions (most recent first). Each has resource_pid / resource_type, amount_cents, period_start / period_end, and status: `applied` (charge deducted) or `skipped` (insufficient balance - the resource was stopped).

tools.name: create_topup
tools.description: Buy wallet credit. Creates a Razorpay hosted payment link and returns a `payment_url` the user must open in a browser to pay - the MCP can't complete the payment. The wallet is credited once Razorpay confirms (webhook), so poll `get_wallet_balance` afterwards. Amount is in cents (min $5 = 500, max $500 = 50000). Requires a linked card: a 402 BILLING_REQUIRED means call `link_billing_payment_method` first.

tools.name: link_billing_payment_method
tools.description: Initiate Razorpay payment-method linking. Returns a `short_url` the user must open in a browser to add a card / UPI. Until they do, paid features stay locked. `billing_contact_phone` is required; tax_id / country_code / state_code are optional and only used for invoices.

billing_email.description: Defaults to the current user's email on the BE if omitted

country_code.description: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2, e.g. IN, US, GB

state_code.description: ISO 3166-2 region code, e.g. KA for Karnataka

tools.name: update_billing_contact
tools.description: Update billing contact info on an already-linked org. Doesn't re-run Razorpay - only persists DB overrides for invoices.

tools.name: list_server_types
tools.description:
List the server sizes a PaaS project can be provisioned on, per location, with live availability and pricing. Public reference data - no org needed, and it does not count against the rate limit.

Returns all six locations - `fsn1` Falkenstein, Germany, `nbg1` Nuremberg, Germany, `hel1` Helsinki, Finland, `ash` Ashburn, Virginia, USA, `hil` Hillsboro, Oregon, USA, `sin` Singapore - each with the sizes sold there: code, cores, memory_gb, disk_gb, `category`, `cpu_type`, `architecture`, `offered`, `available`, `deprecated` + `deprecation`, `hourly_price_cents` and a formatted `display_price`. Prices are all-in (platform margin already folded in) and billed hourly against wallet credit.

PRICES DIFFER PER LOCATION for the same size, so always name the location alongside a price. `cx*` Cost-Optimized (`cost_optimized`) is sold in the three European locations only. `cpx*` Regular (`regular_purpose`) comes in two generations that never share a location: the `cpx*2` line sells in Europe + Singapore, and the `cpx*1` line is listed everywhere but in practice only carries stock in the two US locations. `ccx*` Dedicated (`general_purpose`) is sold in all six. The two Regular generations are NOT interchangeable: cpx21 is 3 cores / 80 GB where cpx22 is 2 cores / 80 GB, and cpx41 is 240 GB where cpx42 is 320 GB.

Because of that geography, the cheapest US or APAC option is several times the cheapest European one. Say so up front rather than letting the user discover it after they pick a region.

Availability is three states, not two. `offered: false` means Hetzner does not sell that size in that location at all - do not offer it there, and do not read the `null` `available` beside it as "out of stock". `offered: true, available: false` means it IS sold there but has no stock right now; that is a one-tap correction (name a location that does have it), not a dead end. Only `available: true` can be provisioned.

Stock genuinely flaps - successive reads minutes apart disagree - so treat availability as live, re-read before acting on it, and never cache it into advice. Expect the cheap end to be the tightest: it is normal for most of the Cost-Optimized line to be out of stock across all three European locations at once, leaving cx23 as the only cheap size that can actually be provisioned.

`deprecated: true` means Hetzner has announced an end of life for that size but still sells it; `deprecation` carries the detail. Do not put a user's new project on one.

Call this before `create_project` and show the user the options - the project server is the main cost of a project, and `create_project` defaults to the smallest (cx23) in Europe if you don't choose.

tools.name: list_projects
tools.description:
List PaaS projects (app containers) in the active organization. Each project is a provisioned server + Coolify install that deployments and project databases attach to.

Returns pid, name, status (`pending` | `provisioning` | `active` | `failed` | `stopped` - `deleting` and `terminated` are filtered out server-side), `public_ip`, `instance_domain`, timestamps, and - the fields worth reading that are easy to miss - `server_type` and `location` (which machine, and WHERE it runs), `backups_enabled`, plus a server-computed `ready` and `readiness_detail`.

`ready` IS NOT `status == "active"`. A project is ready only when it is active, carries no terminal error, AND every service and database inside it is ready too. So an `active` project can still be not-ready because something in it is mid-provision. `readiness_detail` lists each child service and database with its own status - use that to say what is holding a project up instead of reporting it as broken.

Answer "where does this run?" from `location`, not from the user's guess: a server cannot be moved after creation, and its price depends on where it is.

tools.name: get_project
tools.description:
Get one project by pid. Use this to POLL provisioning progress after `create_project`: re-call every ~5-10s until `status` becomes `active` (the server and Coolify are up, deployments can be created) or `failed`. A `status` of `deleting`, or a 404, means it is being or has been torn down. `public_ip` and `instance_domain` populate during provisioning.

TWO DIFFERENT QUESTIONS, TWO DIFFERENT FIELDS:
- `status == "active"` - the project's own server is up. This is what gates `create_deployment`.
- `ready` - active AND no terminal error AND every service and database inside the project is also ready. This is what gates telling the user "your project is up".
An active-but-not-ready project is normal while a service is still booting; `readiness_detail` names the child that is holding it.

Also here and worth reporting: `location` (where the server actually runs - a server cannot be moved, and the price follows the location), `server_type`, and `backups_enabled`.

If a project has been provisioning for more than ~15 minutes, treat it as stuck rather than slow. `list_project_activities` shows what the server and the platform were doing.

tools.name: create_project
tools.description:
Create a new PaaS project and start async server provisioning. Returns immediately (HTTP 202) with the project in status `pending` - actual provisioning (server → Coolify → DNS) takes ~2-5 minutes. Poll `get_project` until status is `active` before creating a deployment in it. Name must be unique within the org (excluding failed/terminated projects). May return 422 if the platform is at capacity for new servers - retry later.

SIZE IT DELIBERATELY: `server_type` decides what the project costs, and omitting it silently provisions the smallest size (cx23, 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk (shared CPU)). Call `list_server_types` for live prices/availability and confirm the choice with the user first. Sizes: cx23 (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk (shared CPU)); cx33 (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk (shared CPU)); cx43 (8 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 160 GB disk (shared CPU)); cx53 (16 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 320 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx21 (3 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 80 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx22 (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 80 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx31 (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 160 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx32 (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 160 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx41 (8 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 240 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx42 (8 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 320 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx51 (16 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 360 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx52 (12 vCPU, 24 GB RAM, 480 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx62 (16 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 640 GB disk (shared CPU)); ccx13 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk (dedicated CPU)); ccx23 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 160 GB disk (dedicated CPU)); ccx33 (8 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 240 GB disk (dedicated CPU)); ccx43 (16 vCPU, 64 GB RAM, 360 GB disk (dedicated CPU)); ccx53 (32 vCPU, 128 GB RAM, 600 GB disk (dedicated CPU)); ccx63 (48 vCPU, 192 GB RAM, 960 GB disk (dedicated CPU)).

PLACE IT DELIBERATELY: `location` decides where the server runs AND what it costs - the same size is a different price in different locations, and the cheap Cost-Optimized line is sold in Europe only. Omitting it lets the platform pick. A server cannot be moved afterwards, and there is no scaling path for a project server either, so the size and the place you choose here are both effectively permanent.

CHECK STOCK FIRST. A cheap size is frequently out of stock in every location that sells it, so a `server_type` chosen from the list above without reading `available` will often 422. When that happens the 422 names the locations that do have it - use them rather than silently falling back.

BACK IT UP AT CREATE: `backups_requested` turns on automatic daily server backups (7 kept) as soon as the server exists. It is FREE - there is no backup SKU for projects, so it adds nothing to the bill. Recommend it for anything that will hold data. It can also be turned on later with `enable_project_backups`.

COSTS MONEY: the server bills hourly against wallet credit from the moment provisioning starts. A 402 means the wallet is empty or no payment method is linked (`create_topup` / `link_billing_payment_method`).

name.description: Project name; unique per org, <=255 chars

backups_requested.description: Enable automatic daily server backups (7 kept) once provisioned. Free - no backup charge for projects. Defaults to off.

server_type.description: Server size to provision. Defaults to cx23 (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk (shared CPU)) - ask the user rather than accepting the default silently.

location.description: Where the server runs: fsn1 (Falkenstein, Germany), nbg1 (Nuremberg, Germany), hel1 (Helsinki, Finland), ash (Ashburn, Virginia, USA), hil (Hillsboro, Oregon, USA), sin (Singapore). A location you name is honoured or refused with a 422 - never silently swapped - so an unavailable (server_type, location) pair fails and names locations that would work. Omit to let the platform place it, which picks the first location with stock. A server CANNOT be moved afterwards, and the price is the price of the location it runs in.

tools.name: update_project
tools.description: Update a project's name and/or description. Only these two fields are editable - status, IPs, and domain are server-managed. Name must remain unique within the org.

name.description: New name (required by the backend even if unchanged)

description.description: New description; pass null to clear

tools.name: delete_project
tools.description: Delete a project - tears down its provisioned server, Coolify install, DNS, and all attached deployments/databases/services. This is irreversible. Returns 202 (async tear-down; status moves to `deleting` then `terminated`). Blocked with 409 if the project is still `pending`/`provisioning`/`deleting`, or if it has an active deployment with a running container - pause active deployments first.

name.description: Project name for the confirmation message (cosmetic)

confirm.description: Must be true. Permanently destroys the server and everything in the project.

tools.name: get_project_metrics
tools.description: Get time-series infrastructure metrics for a project (server CPU/memory/disk/network, plus per-database and per-deployment container metrics) sourced from the project's monitoring agent heartbeats. Returns `agent_status`, `last_seen_at`, and a `batches` array. Each batch has `timestamp_ms` and `metric_sets`; a metric set with no `resource` belongs to the server, otherwise `resource.pid` identifies the database/service/deployment it describes. For a 'current' snapshot use a narrow window and read the newest batch. Heartbeats land ~every 25s, so poll no faster than ~30s.

tools.name: list_deployments
tools.description: List deployments (apps) in the active organization. Each entry includes repo_full_name, branch, build_pack, port, status (active | paused - the container lifecycle, distinct from a run's status), deploy_url, custom domains, and an inline `deployment_runs` array (newest 50). Run status values: `enqueued`/`building`/`deploying` are in-progress (transient); `active` = deployed successfully; `failed`/`aborted`/`removed`/`skipped` are terminal. Poll until the latest run reaches a terminal status.

is_preview.description: If set, filter by preview-deployment flag

tools.name: get_deployment
tools.description: Get one deployment by pid, including its inline build/run history (`deployment_runs`, newest 50) and the `current_deployment_run_pid`. Use this to POLL deploy progress after `trigger_deploy`/`redeploy_run`/`rollback_run`: re-call every ~5s until the latest run reaches a terminal status. Run status values: `enqueued`/`building`/`deploying` are in-progress (transient); `active` = deployed successfully; `failed`/`aborted`/`removed`/`skipped` are terminal. Poll until the latest run reaches a terminal status.

tools.name: create_deployment
tools.description:
Create a deployment (app) from a GitHub repo inside an existing project. The project (`coolify_project_pid`) MUST already be `active` (provisioned) - check `get_project` first. For private repos you must pass `installation_id` (from `list_github_installations`). If build_pack/port are omitted they are auto-detected (you can pre-run `detect_repo_config`).

THIS IS ASYNCHRONOUS AND THE 201 IS NOT THE FINISHED ARTICLE. The request validates and detects synchronously, then saves the deployment as status `provisioning` and does the app registration (9-11 Coolify calls, more for a private repo) in a background job before triggering the first build. So the response you get back has `coolify_app_uuid: null` and `deploy_url: null`. That is expected, not a failure - DO NOT report a broken deployment or retry the create.

Poll `get_deployment` until status is `active` (the app is registered, the URL is populated, the first build is running) or `failed` (registration failed; the run carries the error). It used to be synchronous and would 504 at the 30s gateway timeout on private repos, which is why it moved.

coolify_project_pid.description: Target project pid; must be status `active`

branch.description: Branch to deploy; defaults to the repo's default branch

installation_id.description: GitHub App installation numeric id; required for private repos

dockerfile_location.description: Path to Dockerfile (when build_pack=dockerfile and it's nested)

env_vars.description: Initial environment variables { KEY: value }. Keys must match ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$; values must be non-empty.

required_env_vars.description: Keys that must be present and non-blank in env_vars

custom_domain.description: Custom domain to attach after creation

tools.name: update_deployment
tools.description: Update a deployment's lifecycle/routing settings: pause/resume (`status`), toggle GitHub-push auto-deploy, set ignore_paths, or cap concurrent preview deployments. Pass at least one field. To change build settings (build_pack/port/base_directory) use `update_deployment_build_config` instead. Pausing blocks deploys until resumed.

ignore_paths.description: Paths excluded from auto-deploy triggers (replaces the list)

tools.name: update_deployment_build_config
tools.description: Update a deployment's build configuration: build_pack, base_directory, port, dockerfile_location, and/or env_vars. The deployment must be provisioned (have a Coolify app) - otherwise returns 422. WARNING: if `env_vars` is provided it FULLY REPLACES the variable set (keys not included are deleted); to add/edit without deleting, use `set_env_vars`/`merge_env_vars` instead. Pass at least one field.

env_vars.description: FULL REPLACEMENT of all env vars { KEY: value }

tools.name: delete_deployment
tools.description: Delete a deployment and its Coolify app, build history, env vars, and attached domains. Irreversible.

name.description: Repo/app name for the confirmation message (cosmetic)

confirm.description: Must be true. Removes the app and all its data.

tools.name: trigger_deploy
tools.description: Trigger a manual deploy of a deployment's current branch (creates a new build run). Returns 409 if a deploy is already in progress (one deploy at a time), or 422 if the deployment is paused or not yet provisioned. Poll `get_deployment` for the new run's progress.

tools.name: get_deployment_health
tools.description: Get a deployment's health: whether the deploy_url is reachable, when it was last checked, any error, and the attached domains.

tools.name: get_run_logs
tools.description:
Get the full build + container logs for one deployment run, plus the run object. This is the ONLY log surface - there is no separate application-log tool, because the backend returns the running container's stdout/stderr here alongside the build output.

Use it for runtime debugging too, not just builds: pass the newest run pid (from `get_deployment`) to see why a deployed app is failing. If the container is crash-looping, the response falls back to the output captured while it was last reachable; if there is nothing at all, the backend synthesizes one line carrying the container's health status instead of returning empty.

The returned log buffer is cumulative and idempotent - each call returns the whole buffer, so REPLACE (don't append) on each poll. To stream a live build, re-call every ~5-10s until `deployment_run.status` is terminal. A 422 "Deployment has not started yet" means the run is still enqueued - back off and retry. Run status values: `enqueued`/`building`/`deploying` are in-progress (transient); `active` = deployed successfully; `failed`/`aborted`/`removed`/`skipped` are terminal. Poll until the latest run reaches a terminal status.

run_pid.description: Run pid, e.g. run_01h... (from a deployment's deployment_runs)

tools.name: redeploy_run
tools.description: Re-run a previous build from the SAME commit it used. Useful to retry a failed build or rebuild without a new push. Requires the source run to have a commit SHA, the deployment to be active, and no in-progress run (422 otherwise). Creates a new run; poll `get_deployment`.

run_pid.description: The run to re-run (its commit will be redeployed)

tools.name: rollback_run
tools.description: Roll back by re-deploying the commit from a PRIOR SUCCESSFUL run. Only runs with status `active` (deployed successfully) can be rolled back to - returns 422 otherwise. Requires the deployment to be active and no in-progress run. Creates a new run; poll `get_deployment`.

run_pid.description: A previously-successful run to roll back to (status must be `active`)

tools.name: sync_deployment_domains
tools.description: Set the FULL list of custom domains on a deployment (replaces any existing set - domains not included are removed). Use this to set/change the primary domain or remove several at once. For just adding one domain, prefer `add_deployment_domain`. Each domain that's new auto-creates an org verification record; the response/`get_deployment` then carries the DNS records to add. The deployment must be provisioned (422 otherwise).

is_primary.description: Mark this as the primary domain (at most one)

domains.description: The complete desired domain set; replaces the current set atomically

tools.name: add_deployment_domain
tools.description: Add (append) one custom domain to a deployment as its primary domain, keeping any existing domains. Auto-creates the org verification record and returns the DNS records (TXT + CNAME) to configure. After adding the records at your DNS provider, call `verify_custom_domain`. The deployment must be provisioned (422 otherwise).

tools.name: remove_deployment_domain
tools.description: Remove one custom domain from a deployment. The remaining domains are re-synced and primary metadata updated.

tools.name: verify_custom_domain
tools.description: Check a custom domain's DNS records live and advance its verification. The domain must have been added to a deployment first. Outcomes: `verified` (both TXT + CNAME present → domain goes live with HTTPS); `ownership_verified` (TXT only - add the CNAME); `routing_configured` (CNAME only - add the TXT); or 422 `pending_verification` (neither found yet - DNS can take up to 48h). The `checks` object reports each record's status and expected value.

tools.name: list_custom_domains
tools.description: List all custom-domain verifications for the active organization, with each domain's status (pending_verification | ownership_verified | routing_configured | verified) and when it was verified.

tools.name: list_env_vars
tools.description: List a deployment's environment variables as { key, value } pairs. NOTE: values are returned in cleartext - handle as secrets. Call this before `set_env_vars` so you know the full current set (since `set_env_vars` replaces everything).

tools.name: detect_env_vars
tools.description:
Scan a deployment's repo/branch for the environment variables it expects, and report which are already configured. Read-only - it changes nothing.

Returns `detected_vars` [{ key, hint, source, configured, configured_value }] and a `sources` summary (.env.example, GitHub workflow secrets, CI files, Dockerfile/compose, framework config). `hint` is the placeholder found in the repo - a hint, NOT a real secret, so never set it as a value; ask the user for each missing one.

Use it right after creating a deployment (or when a build fails on a missing variable) to find out what still needs setting, then apply the answers with `merge_env_vars`. Vars already stored come back with configured=true so you can skip them.

tools.name: set_env_vars
tools.description: REPLACE a deployment's ENTIRE set of environment variables with the provided map. ⚠️ Any existing key NOT included here is DELETED. To add or edit a few variables without removing the rest, use `merge_env_vars` instead - or call `list_env_vars` first and pass the full merged set here. Keys must match ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$; values must be non-empty. Saving may trigger a rate-limited redeploy.

env_vars.description: The COMPLETE desired set { KEY: value }; replaces all existing vars

tools.name: merge_env_vars
tools.description: Add or update environment variables WITHOUT deleting any existing ones (upsert/merge). This is the safe way to set a few variables. Keys must match ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$; values must be non-empty. To remove a variable use `delete_env_var`. Saving may trigger a rate-limited redeploy.

env_vars.description: The variables to add/update { KEY: value }; existing keys are preserved

tools.name: delete_env_var
tools.description: Delete a single environment variable by key. Returns 404 if the key doesn't exist. Saving may trigger a rate-limited redeploy.

tools.name: list_github_installations
tools.description: List the GitHub App installations connected to the active organization, each with its accessible repositories embedded (`repos`: name, full_name, url, private, default_branch, description). Use `isActive`/status to pick a usable installation, and the repo's `default_branch` when listing branches. If empty, the org hasn't connected GitHub yet - use `get_github_connect_url`.

tools.name: list_repo_branches
tools.description: List branches of a repository accessible through a GitHub installation. Provide the installation pid (ghi_..., from `list_github_installations`) and the repo as owner/repo. The API does not flag the default branch - cross-reference the repo's `default_branch` from `list_github_installations`.

tools.name: detect_repo_config
tools.description: Scan a GitHub repo and auto-detect how to build/deploy it: visibility (`private`), `build_pack` (nixpacks | dockerfile | dockercompose | static), `port`, `dockerfile_path`, monorepo `base_directories`, and detected environment variables (`detected_vars` from .env.example/CI/workflows - these are hints, not secrets). Run this before `create_deployment` to pre-fill build settings. For PRIVATE repos you must pass `installation_pid` (else 422).

installation_pid.description: Installation pid (ghi_...); required for private repos

branch.description: Branch to scan (defaults to the repo's default branch)

tools.name: get_github_connect_url
tools.description: Get a URL for the human to open in their browser to connect/install the SelfHost GitHub App on their account or org. Connecting GitHub is interactive (GitHub requires a logged-in user to approve and pick repos) and CANNOT be done headlessly. After the user completes it in the browser, poll `list_github_installations` to confirm the new installation appears (status `active`).

redirect_to_frontend.description: Optional URL to return the browser to after install

tools.name: disconnect_github_installation
tools.description: DESTRUCTIVE: disconnect one GitHub App installation from the active organization. Pushes for its repos stop triggering deploys immediately. The backend refuses while deployments are still using the installation - delete or repoint those first. This only detaches it on the SelfHost side; the response includes a GitHub URL the user must open to revoke the app on GitHub itself. Reconnecting later is a browser flow (`get_github_connect_url`).

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed.

tools.name: disconnect_all_github_installations
tools.description: DESTRUCTIVE: disconnect EVERY GitHub App installation from the active organization at once. All auto-deploys stop. Blocked by the backend while any deployment still uses one of them. Returns `disconnected_count` and a `github_revoke_urls` list the user must open to revoke the app on GitHub. Prefer `disconnect_github_installation` when only one account should go.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed.

tools.name: list_project_databases
tools.description:
List the databases attached to a project (Postgres/Redis/MySQL/MongoDB provisioned via Coolify, NOT AWS managed instances). Returns pid, name, db_type, status (`active` | `inactive` | `creating` | `failed` | `unknown`), is_public, public_port, `vector_enabled` / `timescaledb_enabled` on Postgres, and a `provisioning` block with per-stage progress.

Passwords are never returned here. Statuses on this list are the last known values; `get_project_database` re-reads one live from Coolify.

tools.name: get_project_database
tools.description:
Get one project database, with its status re-read LIVE from Coolify rather than served from the last known value. Use this when `list_project_databases` shows `creating` and you need to know whether it has actually finished, or when a status looks stale.

Also returns `vector_enabled` / `timescaledb_enabled` (Postgres) and the `provisioning` stage block, so it is the tool to reach for when a user asks why provisioning is taking so long.

Unlike create, this works on a stopped or billing-suspended project. On one of those the live refresh is skipped (the server is powered off and there is nothing to ask) and you get the stored record - so a `creating` status on a stopped project means "we never found out", not "still working".

Passwords are not returned. Connection details for a project database come from the console.

tools.name: create_project_database
tools.description:
Create a database inside a project (provisioned via Coolify; returns 202, status starts `creating` - poll `list_project_databases`). The project must be `active`. Provide the type-specific credentials (see fields). Passwords must be 8+ chars with no spaces or shell-dangerous chars. `is_public` is REQUIRED and has no default: ASK THE USER whether the database should be publicly reachable on a port (convenient for external clients but exposes it to the internet) or kept private to the project (safer). Do not assume.

POSTGRES EXTENSIONS (create-time only here - unlike AWS instances, a project database cannot gain an extension later; you would have to recreate it):
- timescaledb_enabled → runs the TimescaleDB image, then enables the extension once the container is healthy.
- vector_enabled → runs the pgvector image, then enables the extension.
- Only ONE image can win: setting both gives you TimescaleDB, and pgvector is NOT installed. Use two databases if you need both.
- Either flag pins the container to PostgreSQL 17.
- The extension step needs a reachable database: with is_public=false there is no external URL, so provisioning succeeds but the CREATE EXTENSION is skipped and the user must run it themselves.

is_public.description: Required choice (ask the user, do not assume): true = expose on a public port (internet-reachable); false = private to the project.

public_port.description: Public port when is_public (defaults: pg 5432, redis 6379, mysql 3306, mongo 27017)

timescaledb_enabled.description: postgres only: use the TimescaleDB image (pins PostgreSQL 17) and enable the extension for time-series data. Takes precedence over vector_enabled - only one image can run.

vector_enabled.description: postgres only: use the pgvector image (pins PostgreSQL 17) and enable the extension for embeddings. Ignored if timescaledb_enabled is also set.

tools.name: delete_project_database
tools.description: Delete a project database. The exact current `name` must be supplied and match (a safety check, 422 otherwise). Returns 202 (async tear-down). Irreversible.

name.description: Exact current database name - must match

confirm.description: Must be true. Permanently destroys the database and its data.

tools.name: list_project_services
tools.description:
List the one-click application templates deployed in a project. Returns pid, name, template_type, status (`creating` | `active` | `inactive` | `failed` | `unknown`), is_public, public_port, external_url, `error_message` when it failed, and a `provisioning` block with the per-stage progress.

CREDENTIALS ARE NOT HERE. Use `get_project_service` for those - it is the only endpoint that returns them.

`external_url` can be null on an otherwise `active` service when the project has no usable public IP; that is a real state, not a bug, and the service simply has no public URL to hand out.

A `template_type` you do not recognise means the backend shipped a template newer than this tool. Report the wire string as-is; delete still works on it.

tools.name: get_project_service
tools.description:
Get one deployed service, INCLUDING ITS CREDENTIALS. This is the only endpoint that returns them - `list_project_services` deliberately does not.

Credentials appear once the service reaches `active`; before that the block is simply absent and the right answer is "not ready yet", not an error. What you get depends on the template: Supabase returns the dashboard username and password plus `public_url` (and the anon key when present); n8n, n8n-with-postgresql and Twenty return `public_url` only, because their first admin is created through the app's own first-run screen rather than from env.

HAND THE URL OVER WITH THE WARNING ATTACHED for n8n and Twenty: the account is claimed by whoever opens it first, so an unattended public URL is an open door until the user completes setup.

Call this after `create_project_service` reports `active`, and give the user the credentials - creating a service and not passing on how to log into it leaves the job half done.

tools.name: create_project_service
tools.description:
Deploy a one-click application template into a project. FOUR are available:

- `supabase` - Postgres + Studio + auth/storage/realtime. The ONLY one that takes admin credentials up front: `dashboard_username` and `dashboard_password` (8+ chars) are REQUIRED and become the Studio login. Boots in about 5 minutes.
- `n8n` - workflow automation, data in a bundled SQLite volume. Name only.
- `n8n-with-postgresql` - the same n8n, backed by a per-service PostgreSQL sidecar instead of SQLite. Pick this for anything beyond light use; the difference is durability and concurrency, and it cannot be switched afterwards. Name only.
- `twenty` - open-source CRM. Name only. Boots in up to 15 minutes (images + migrations) - do not declare it stuck early.

FIRST-ADMIN WARNING for n8n, n8n-with-postgresql and Twenty: these have no admin credentials at all. The first person to open the public URL gets the owner account. Tell the user to complete setup immediately, and do not post the URL anywhere until they have. Passing `dashboard_username`/`dashboard_password` to them does nothing - they are rejected here rather than sent and silently ignored.

`is_public` is REQUIRED with no default: ASK THE USER. These are web apps whose first-run setup happens at the public URL, so `true` is usually what they want, but do not assume it.

The project must be `active` (409 otherwise). Returns 202 with status `creating`; poll `list_project_services`, then call `get_project_service` for the credentials once it is `active`.

EXPECT THESE 422s: a duplicate service name inside the same project; `public_port` already claimed by another database or service in the project; and the host being out of RAM (a capacity guard refuses new services rather than thrashing the box - the fix is a bigger project server, and there is no in-place resize for projects, so it means a new project).

is_public.description: Required choice (ask the user, do not assume): true = internet-reachable; false = private to the project. First-run setup for these apps happens at the public URL.
