dashboard_username.description: Supabase ONLY - the Studio dashboard username. Required for supabase, rejected for every other template.

dashboard_password.description: Supabase ONLY - the Studio dashboard password, 8+ chars. Required for supabase, rejected for every other template.

public_port.description: Optional. Must not collide with another database or service in this project.

tools.name: delete_project_service
tools.description: Delete a project service. The exact current `name` must be supplied and match (a safety check, 422 otherwise). Returns 202 (async tear-down) and removes the service's volumes, configs and networks along with it. Irreversible. Works on any template_type, including one this tool does not recognise.

name.description: Exact current service name - must match

confirm.description: Must be true. Permanently destroys the service and its data.

tools.name: list_deployment_notification_bindings
tools.description: List the notification channels bound to a deployment (which channels get notified when a deploy succeeds/fails/aborts). Returns binding_pid, notification_channel_pid, channel_type, name, and bound_at.

tools.name: bind_deployment_notification_channel
tools.description: Bind an existing org notification channel to a deployment so it's notified on deploy outcomes. The channel pid (nchan_...) comes from `list_notification_channels` (create one with `create_notification_channel` if needed). Returns 422 if already bound, 404 if the channel doesn't exist. Org owner only.

notification_channel_pid.description: Org notification channel pid, e.g. nchan_...

tools.name: unbind_deployment_notification_channel
tools.description: Unbind a notification channel from a deployment (it will no longer be notified on deploy outcomes). Pass the notification_channel_pid (NOT the binding pid). Org owner only.

notification_channel_pid.description: The notification channel pid (nchan_...) to unbind

tools.name: list_project_backups
tools.description:
List the automatic backups of a project's server, read live from Hetzner.

Returns `backups_enabled`, a `backup_schedule` (`cadence`, `retention`, and the UTC window) and the `backups` themselves. Each backup carries the image id you pass to `restore_project_backup`.

Backups are daily and seven are kept - both fixed, neither configurable. Hetzner assigns the daily window shortly AFTER backups are switched on, so a just-enabled project can legitimately report the cadence and retention with a null window; that is "window pending", not a fault.

This is a read and works on a stopped or billing-suspended project, so it is safe to call when a project is in trouble and the user is deciding whether they can recover it.

Backups cost the customer nothing - the platform absorbs the provider charge. Do not quote a backup price.

tools.name: enable_project_backups
tools.description:
Turn on automatic daily backups of a project's server. Seven are kept, on a window Hetzner assigns shortly after this call.

FREE. There is no backup SKU for projects, so this adds nothing to the bill - the platform absorbs the provider cost. Say that plainly if the user asks what it costs; do not hedge with a percentage.

Given that, this is close to a straight win for any project holding real data, and worth recommending when a user has databases or services in a project with backups off.

The project must be `active`. A 409 means the project is not `active` yet (or its server is not up) - wait, do not retry in a loop. A 502 means Hetzner refused the operation.

Returns 202. Confirm with `list_project_backups`; the first backup appears after the first window passes, not immediately.

tools.name: disable_project_backups
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: turn off automatic backups for a project AND DELETE THE BACKUPS ALREADY TAKEN. Hetzner removes them with the schedule; there is no pause that keeps them and no way to get them back.

So this is not "stop making new backups" - it is "stop, and throw away every restore point this project has". Check with the user that they mean both. If they only want to stop paying for something, tell them backups are free and there is nothing to save.

The project must be `active`. A 409 means the project is not `active` yet (or its server is not up) - wait, do not retry in a loop. A 502 means Hetzner refused the operation.

You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

confirm.description: Must be true. Deletes every existing backup of this project, irreversibly.

tools.name: restore_project_backup
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: rebuild a project's server from one of its backups. The VM's boot disk is overwritten, so EVERYTHING on it goes back to the state it was in when that backup was taken - the Coolify install, every service, and every project database, including anything written since.

This is a real rollback, unlike the ClickHouse data restore in `restore_backup` which merges. Data created after the chosen backup is gone and cannot be recovered.

The project goes to status `restoring` and is UNAVAILABLE while the server is rebuilt. Every app and database in it is down for the duration.

Requires `image_id` from `list_project_backups`, and `name` must exactly match the project's current name (422 otherwise) - that check exists so a restore cannot be fired at the wrong project. Backups must be enabled.

A 409 means the project is not `active` yet (or its server is not up) - wait, do not retry in a loop. A 502 means Hetzner refused the operation.

Before calling: show the user the backup list with dates, get them to pick, and state what they will lose. You MUST set confirm=true.

image_id.description: The backup image to restore, from `list_project_backups`

name.description: The project's exact current name - must match or the backend refuses

confirm.description: Must be true. Overwrites the server's disk; everything written since this backup is lost.

tools.name: list_project_activities
tools.description:
The history of what has happened to a project, newest first. This is the tool for "why did my project go down", "when was this restarted", "who deleted that service" - questions no other project tool can answer.

Two sources merged into one chronological, paginated feed, each item tagged with `source`:
- `hetzner` - infrastructure actions on the server itself: create_server, rebuild, enable_backup, assign_primary_ip and so on.
- `platform` - our own events: backups, restores, deployments, provisioning stages, lifecycle changes including credit-driven stops.

Reading them together is the point. A project that stopped answering shows the platform event and the server action side by side, which is usually enough to tell "we stopped it for billing" from "the machine was rebuilt".

If Hetzner is unreachable the feed degrades to platform events only and sets `meta.server_activities_available: false` rather than failing. Check that flag before concluding nothing happened at the infrastructure level - an empty infra history and an unavailable one look identical otherwise.

Works on a stopped or billing-suspended project.

page.description: 1-based page number; omit for the first (newest) page

tools.name: get_proxysql
tools.description: Get the ProxySQL connection-pooling config and status for a MySQL instance. Returns null when pooling has never been configured. ProxySQL status: disabled | enabling | enabled | disabling | error.

tools.name: enable_proxysql
tools.description: Enable ProxySQL connection pooling on a MySQL instance (MySQL-only). Clients connect on port 6033 once status reaches `enabled`; the ProxySQL admin interface listens on port 6032. Status is one of disabled | enabling | enabled | disabling | error. After enabling, poll `get_proxysql` until status is `enabled`.

multiplexing.description: Reuse backend connections across clients when safe

connection_max_age_ms.description: Max age of a backend connection in milliseconds before recycling (>= 0)

tools.name: reconfigure_proxysql
tools.description: Apply new ProxySQL settings on an already-enabled MySQL instance. Only sends the fields you provide (PATCH-style). Status must be `enabled`; will return an error otherwise.

tools.name: disable_proxysql
tools.description: Disable ProxySQL on a MySQL instance. Existing connections drain gracefully. The config row is preserved so you can re-enable later with `enable_proxysql`. Valid from `enabled` or `error` state - use this to recover from `error`.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Disabling will drop pool warmth and force clients back to port 3306.

tools.name: get_mysql_config
tools.description: Get the current MySQL configuration for a running instance, showing calculated defaults, overrides, and effective values.

tools.name: update_mysql_config
tools.description: Update MySQL configuration parameters on a running instance. Set a value to null to revert to the calculated default. max_connections and innodb_buffer_pool_size require an instance restart.

max_connections.description: Max concurrent connections (e.g. 151). Set null to revert to default. Requires restart.

innodb_buffer_pool_size.description: InnoDB buffer pool memory (e.g. '256MB'). Set null to revert. Requires restart.

tmp_table_size.description: Max size of in-memory internal temp tables (e.g. '16MB'). Set null to revert.

wait_timeout.description: Seconds an idle connection is kept before it is closed (e.g. 28800). Set null to revert.

tools.name: get_chproxy
tools.description:
Get the CHProxy connection-pooling config for a ClickHouse instance. Returns null when pooling has never been configured. Status: disabled | enabling | enabled | disabling | error (with error_message).

The same payload is embedded as `chproxy_config` on every instance response, so get_instance already tells you the state if you have the instance in hand.

tools.name: enable_chproxy
tools.description:
Enable CHProxy connection pooling on a ClickHouse instance - the ClickHouse counterpart to PgBouncer/ProxySQL. Clients connect over HTTP on port 9090 once status reaches `enabled` (poll via get_chproxy); the native TCP port 9000 is unaffected. Defaults: max_concurrent_queries=100, max_queue_size=200, max_queue_time=30, max_execution_time=0 (unlimited).

ClickHouse instances only. The instance must be running/provisioned with a live agent.

max_concurrent_queries.description: Max simultaneous queries per user (default 100, range 1-2000)

max_queue_size.description: Max queries queued once the concurrency limit is hit (default 200, range 0-10000; 0 = reject immediately)

max_queue_time.description: Seconds a query waits in the queue before rejection (default 30, range 0-3600)

max_execution_time.description: Max query execution time in seconds (default 0 = no limit, range 0-86400)

tools.name: reconfigure_chproxy
tools.description: Apply new CHProxy settings to a ClickHouse instance. Only sends the fields you provide; omitted fields keep their current values. Valid from `enabled`, `enabling` or `error` - use it to retry a failed enable without disabling first.

max_concurrent_queries.description: Max simultaneous queries per user (default 100, range 1-2000)

max_queue_size.description: Max queries queued once the concurrency limit is hit (default 200, range 0-10000; 0 = reject immediately)

max_queue_time.description: Seconds a query waits in the queue before rejection (default 30, range 0-3600)

max_execution_time.description: Max query execution time in seconds (default 0 = no limit, range 0-86400)

tools.name: disable_chproxy
tools.description: Disable CHProxy on a ClickHouse instance. The config row is preserved so you can re-enable later with enable_chproxy. Valid from `enabled` or `error` - use this to clear a stuck error state.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Clients pooling on port 9090 must move back to the direct HTTP port 8123.

tools.name: enable_timescaledb
tools.description:
Enable the TimescaleDB extension on an existing PostgreSQL instance - hypertables, continuous aggregates, compression, and retention policies for time-series data.

What happens: the APT package is installed, `timescaledb` is added to shared_preload_libraries, **PostgreSQL is restarted once**, and `CREATE EXTENSION timescaledb` runs. The instance enters `updating` while the `postgres_enable_timescaledb` task runs - poll get_instance to follow it.

IRREVERSIBLE: TimescaleDB cannot be disabled afterwards (the backend 422s on any attempt). PostgreSQL only, and the instance needs a registered agent.

To start a new instance with it already installed, pass timescaledb_enabled to create_instance instead - no restart needed that way. Once installed, these metrics join the instance's `postgresql.database` alert set: timescaledb_hypertable_count, timescaledb_chunk_count, timescaledb_compressed_chunk_count, timescaledb_compression_ratio, timescaledb_total_size_bytes.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user first: this restarts PostgreSQL once and can never be undone.

tools.name: enable_pgvector
tools.description:
Enable the pgvector extension on an existing PostgreSQL instance - the `vector` column type plus similarity search for embeddings.

What happens: `CREATE EXTENSION vector` runs and pgvector's parameter overrides are applied without a restart (tasks `postgres_enable_pgvector` then `postgres_config_update`). The instance enters `updating` while they run - poll get_instance.

IRREVERSIBLE: pgvector cannot be disabled afterwards (the backend 422s on any attempt). PostgreSQL only, and the instance needs a registered agent.

To start a new instance with it already installed, pass vector_enabled to create_instance instead.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user first: this changes Postgres config and can never be undone.

tools.name: set_postgres_tls
tools.description:
Turn client TLS on or off for a PostgreSQL instance group - encryption in transit between clients and the database.

WHOLE GROUP, ONE CALL. TLS is group state, so this covers the primary and every replica together; there is no per-replica setting. Certificates are issued lazily per group.

Enabling is the right default for anything a client connects to over a network the user does not control, and worth recommending if a production Postgres has it off. Once on, clients should connect with `sslmode=require` (or stricter) - a client left on the default may keep connecting in the clear.

TURNING IT OFF is a downgrade, not a cleanup: connections go back to plaintext and any client pinned to `sslmode=require` starts failing. Confirm the user means it.

Postgres ONLY (422 on any other engine). The instance must be `running` or `provisioned` and must have a registered agent. Fan-out is dispatched as tasks; a response saying TLS is "already" in that state is a no-op, not a failure.

AFTER A RESTORE OR A FORK, TLS IS OFF even if the source had it on - the new group starts without a certificate. Re-enable it explicitly and tell the user, because a restored instance silently serving plaintext is the kind of thing nobody checks.

tls_enabled.description: true = require/allow TLS for client connections across the group; false = back to plaintext

confirm.description: Required only when turning TLS OFF, since that downgrades every client connection in the group.

tools.name: list_log_sources
tools.description:
List the log sources available on a managed database instance. Call this before `fetch_instance_logs` - the valid `log_source` values are per engine and per instance.

Log sources differ per engine and `list_log_sources` is the only authority - do not guess a name, an unknown one is a 422. Every engine has `engine` (the server's own log) and a `replication` view; Postgres and MySQL add backup/restore logs, and ClickHouse adds separate backup, native-restore, fork and upgrade logs. `replication` is a server-side FILTERED view of the engine log rather than a separate file on Postgres and MySQL, so it is the right source for a replication question and will look like a subset of `engine`.

Returns `{sources: [{key, label}]}`. An EMPTY list means the engine does not support log tailing at all (only Postgres, MySQL and ClickHouse do) - it does not mean something went wrong.

A 422 saying to top up means the organization's wallet is empty. This endpoint is behind the same balance gate as the fetch itself, so an empty source list and a billing block are different answers: read the message.

tools.name: fetch_instance_logs
tools.description:
Ask the instance for the tail of one of its logs. This is how you actually look at a database that is misbehaving - no SSH needed.

TWO STEPS. This POST creates a PENDING fetch and returns immediately; the agent on the box collects the output and posts it back a moment later. Read it with `list_instance_log_fetches`. The response here almost never contains the log text.

Log sources differ per engine and `list_log_sources` is the only authority - do not guess a name, an unknown one is a 422. Every engine has `engine` (the server's own log) and a `replication` view; Postgres and MySQL add backup/restore logs, and ClickHouse adds separate backup, native-restore, fork and upgrade logs. `replication` is a server-side FILTERED view of the engine log rather than a separate file on Postgres and MySQL, so it is the right source for a replication question and will look like a subset of `engine`.

`lines` defaults to 200 and is clamped to 2000. Output is capped at 1 MB per fetch, so a very chatty log is truncated rather than refused - ask for fewer lines and a specific source if you are hunting something particular.

DEDUP AND COOLDOWN, both worth understanding before you loop:
- A pending fetch for the same source is returned as-is instead of a second one being started. So an immediate repeat call is a no-op, not progress.
- After a fetch completes or fails there is a ~10s cooldown per (instance, source) and a further request is rate-limited.
So: request once, wait, then read. Do not poll this endpoint.

Requires the instance to be `running` or `provisioned`, with a registered agent, and `cloud_instances:update` (a 403 means the caller's role is too low - reading the result needs only view access). Replicas are fine.

log_source.description: A `key` from `list_log_sources` for this instance. Guessing gets a 422.

lines.description: Tail length; defaults to 200, clamped to 2000

tools.name: list_instance_log_fetches
tools.description:
Read the results of log fetches on an instance - the last 20, newest first, WITH their output. This is where the log text you asked for with `fetch_instance_logs` actually shows up.

Each row: `pid`, `log_source`, `lines_requested`, `status`, `output`, `error`, and timestamps.

`status` is `pending` until the agent reports back, then `completed` (read `output`) or `failed` (read `error`). A fetch whose agent result was lost is flipped to `failed` when you read this endpoint rather than sitting pending forever - so reading is also how a stuck fetch gets cleared.

Because the backend keeps the last 20 per instance, previous fetches are already here: check them before requesting a new one, since a recent fetch of the same source may answer the question and avoid the cooldown entirely.

Output can be up to 1 MB. Summarise what matters to the user rather than replaying the whole tail.

tools.name: capture_db_stats
tools.description:
Take a query-workload snapshot of a database: what it is actually doing right now. Use this for "why is my database slow" before reaching for metrics - metrics say the CPU is busy, this says which queries are making it busy.

SAMPLES OVER TIME. The agent reads the engine's cumulative counters twice, `sample_seconds` apart, and reports the difference - so the result describes that window, not a single instant. Default 10s, allowed 5 to 60. A longer sample smooths out a spiky workload; a short one catches a burst.

Same two-step shape as the logs: this POST returns a PENDING sample, and you read the result with `list_db_stats`. Do not poll this endpoint - a pending sample is returned as-is instead of starting a second one, and there is a per-instance cooldown after one finishes.

Postgres, MySQL and ClickHouse. NOT available on a ClickHouse keeper-only node (a keeper runs clickhouse-keeper, not clickhouse-server, so there is no query log to sample) - that is a 422 and the answer is to target a data node instead. Instance must be `running` or `provisioned` with a registered agent, and this needs `cloud_instances:update`.

sample_seconds.description: Sampling window in seconds; default 10, clamped to 5-60

tools.name: list_db_stats
tools.description:
Read query-workload samples for an instance - the last 20, newest first, with their results. This is where a `capture_db_stats` sample lands.

Each row: `pid`, `sample_seconds`, `status`, `stats`, `error`, and timestamps. `status` is `pending` until the agent reports, then `completed` (read `stats`) or `failed` (read `error`).

Check here first: a recent sample may already answer the question, and reusing it avoids both the sampling wait and the cooldown.

Remember what the numbers are - a delta over the sample window, not lifetime totals - so "queries per second" figures are for that window only and a quiet moment will understate a workload the user is complaining about. If the numbers look implausibly calm, take a longer sample while the problem is happening rather than concluding the database is fine.

tools.name: list_capacity_ladders
tools.description:
List the machine-size ladders a database engine can be scaled along. A ladder is an ordered list of instance types, and every tier bound elsewhere in this module is an INDEX into it - so read this before setting or interpreting `min_tier_index` / `max_tier_index`.

Returns `profiles` keyed by profile name, each an array of `{index, instance_type, vcpu, memory_gib}`:
- `default` - the data plane's ladder.
- `auxiliary` - the ladder for non-data nodes (ClickHouse keepers).

A 404 means no ladder is configured for that engine and provider, which means tier scaling is not available for it - not that something failed. Ladders exist for AWS; Hetzner has definitions but no execution in this version.

Cheap and stable: fetch it once and reuse it while you reason about tiers, rather than per question.

cloud_provider.description: Defaults to `aws`, which is the only provider that executes tier moves today

tools.name: get_capacity_config
tools.description:
Read a group's tier-scaling guardrails, where it currently sits on the ladder, and any scale plan in flight. This is the tool for "is my cluster scaling?" and "why is it stuck?".

Returns `config` (bounds, profile, enabled), `current_tier_index` and `current_instance_type`, the `resolved_ladder`, and every instance in scope with its own tier index.

Plus, when the data plane is involved:
- `active_scale_plan` - a move in progress, with `ordered_node_replacements` so you can say which node is being replaced and how many remain. This is what makes the zero-downtime claim checkable rather than a promise.
- `last_failed_scale_plan` - READ THIS WHENEVER SCALING SEEMS DEAD. A failed plan BLOCKS all further automatic scaling for the group until it is retried or deleted, and nothing else surfaces it. Its `error_message` says why, and `retry_cluster_scale_plan` / `delete_cluster_scale_plan` are how you clear it.
- `active_tier_event` / `last_tier_event` - the equivalent for a SINGLE-NODE group, which moves tier via an in-place resize and produces no plan object at all. On a single-node cluster these are the only progress you get, so do not conclude "nothing is happening" from an absent plan.

A 404 means no config exists for that group (or you own no instances in it) - the group simply is not set up for tier scaling, which is a normal state and the answer to give.

group_id.description: The instance group id (from an instance's `group_id`)

tools.name: create_capacity_config
tools.description:
Set up tier-scaling guardrails for an instance group: the floor and ceiling it may move between on the machine-size ladder.

Guardrails and triggers are separate. This config only says HOW FAR the group may move; nothing moves until a tier policy says WHEN. Create the config first (a policy against a missing or disabled config is refused), then `create_scaling_policy` with `scaling_action: "resize_instance"`, `group_id`, `target_class`, and a `direction` of `scale_up` or `scale_down`.

`min_tier_index` and `max_tier_index` are indexes into the ladder from `list_capacity_ladders` - fetch that first and show the user the actual machine types the bounds correspond to. A ceiling is a spend ceiling: state what the top tier costs before setting it, because automatic scaling will use it.

`profile` is normally left out and defaulted server-side from `target_class` (`data` to `default`, `non_data` to `auxiliary`). Only set it if you specifically mean to use a different ladder.

`deprecation_window_minutes` is how long a replaced node is kept before teardown - a rollback window. Too short and a bad move cannot be undone; it also means paying for both nodes for that long.

`enabled: false` creates the guardrails without arming anything, which is a reasonable way to stage a setup for review.

AWS and the data plane are what actually execute today.

target_class.description: `data` for the data plane, `non_data` for ClickHouse keepers (v1 executes data only)

min_tier_index.description: Lowest ladder index the group may scale down to

max_tier_index.description: Highest ladder index it may scale up to - this is a spend ceiling, quote its cost to the user

deprecation_window_minutes.description: How long a replaced node is retained before teardown (rollback window; both nodes bill during it)

enabled.description: Arm the guardrails. false stages the config without allowing any move.

profile.description: Ladder profile. Omit - it is derived from target_class.

tools.name: update_capacity_config
tools.description:
Change a group's tier bounds, rollback window, or whether tier scaling is armed at all.

DO NOT SEND `target_class` FOR A BOUNDS-ONLY CHANGE. Passing it makes the backend re-derive `profile`, which can swap the group onto a different ladder and silently reinterpret every tier index. Send only the fields you are actually changing.

`enabled: false` is the pause: it stops automatic tier moves while keeping the config and its policies intact. Prefer it over deleting.

Raising `max_tier_index` raises the spend ceiling - say what the new top tier costs. Lowering bounds below where the group currently sits does not move it back on its own; a scale-down policy has to fire.

enabled.description: false pauses automatic tier scaling without deleting anything

target_class.description: Leave this OUT unless you intend to change the ladder - sending it re-derives `profile`.

tools.name: delete_capacity_config
tools.description:
Remove a group's tier-scaling guardrails entirely. The group stays on whatever machine size it is on now - nothing is resized - but it loses the ability to move tier automatically.

A 422 means enabled tier policies still reference this config. Delete or disable those policies first (`list_scaling_policies` then `delete_scaling_policy`); the backend refuses rather than leaving triggers pointing at bounds that no longer exist.

If the intent is only to stop automatic scaling, `update_capacity_config` with `enabled: false` does that and keeps the setup. Offer that first.

You MUST set confirm=true.

confirm.description: Must be true. Removes the guardrails; the group's current size is unchanged.

tools.name: retry_cluster_scale_plan
tools.description:
Retry a FAILED cluster scale plan, picking up from where it stopped rather than starting over.

WHY THIS MATTERS: a failed plan blocks every further automatic tier move for its group. A cluster whose scaling has quietly stopped working usually has one of these sitting in `last_failed_scale_plan` on `get_capacity_config`. Retrying or deleting it is what unblocks the group.

Read the plan's `error_message` first and decide whether the cause is likely gone. Retrying into an unchanged cause just fails again; if the underlying problem is permanent, `delete_cluster_scale_plan` is the way to clear the block.

Returns the plan with status `in_progress`. A 422 means it is not in a retryable state - typically already running, or not failed.

tools.name: delete_cluster_scale_plan
tools.description:
Discard a FAILED cluster scale plan, giving up on that move and unblocking automatic tier scaling for the group.

Use this when the plan's failure cause is not going away and `retry_cluster_scale_plan` would just fail again. The group stays on the size it currently has; the abandoned move is simply forgotten.

A 422 means the plan is not failed - only a failed plan may be discarded, so a running one has to finish or fail first. A 404 means it is already gone, which is the outcome you wanted anyway.

You MUST set confirm=true.

confirm.description: Must be true. Abandons the scale attempt; the group keeps its current size.

tools.name: list_webhook_endpoints
tools.description:
List the organization's outgoing webhook endpoints - the HTTPS URLs the platform calls when subscribed events happen.

Each row carries its `pid`, `url` and `subscribed_events`.

Not to be confused with deployment notification channels (`list_deployment_notification_bindings`), which push a specific deployment's outcome to Slack or email. These are org-wide, event-typed HTTP callbacks for a receiver you run.

tools.name: get_webhook_endpoint
tools.description: Get one webhook endpoint - its URL and the events it is subscribed to. Use it to check what a receiver will actually be told before changing anything.

tools.name: create_webhook_endpoint
tools.description:
Register an HTTPS URL to receive platform events for this organization.

The URL MUST be HTTPS - plain HTTP is rejected. At least one event is required.

Available events:
- `instance.scaling_failed` - an auto-scale or resize did not complete. The one worth subscribing to for anything production: a failed scale is silent otherwise, and a failed cluster scale plan also blocks all further scaling for that group.
- `deploy_run.succeeded` / `deploy_run.failed` / `deploy_run.aborted` - a build run reached a terminal state. Fires for every deployment in the org, not one app.
- `preview_deployment.created` / `preview_deployment.destroyed` - a per-branch preview environment appeared or went away.
- `database_user.password_rotated` - a database user's password was rotated. THIS IS THE SIGNAL a credential consumer needs when `password_rotation_enabled` is true on that user: the payload never carries the password, so the receiver must refetch with `rotate_database_user_password`. Subscribing to it is what makes automatic rotation safe rather than breaking.

Subscribe deliberately: every event fires for the WHOLE organization, so `deploy_run.*` on a busy org is a lot of traffic to a receiver that only cares about one app.

A signing `secret` is generated server-side at create and is NOT settable. The receiver should verify it - tell the user to grab it from the create response, because that is how they authenticate the calls.

Requires `webhook_endpoints:create` (owner or admin).

url.description: HTTPS URL to POST events to. Plain HTTP is rejected.

subscribed_events.description: Events to send. An unknown event name is rejected with the offending value named.

tools.name: update_webhook_endpoint
tools.description:
Change a webhook endpoint's URL or which events it receives.

`subscribed_events` REPLACES the list, it does not add to it. Read the current set with `get_webhook_endpoint` and send the full intended list, or you will silently unsubscribe the receiver from everything you left out.

Available events:
- `instance.scaling_failed` - an auto-scale or resize did not complete. The one worth subscribing to for anything production: a failed scale is silent otherwise, and a failed cluster scale plan also blocks all further scaling for that group.
- `deploy_run.succeeded` / `deploy_run.failed` / `deploy_run.aborted` - a build run reached a terminal state. Fires for every deployment in the org, not one app.
- `preview_deployment.created` / `preview_deployment.destroyed` - a per-branch preview environment appeared or went away.
- `database_user.password_rotated` - a database user's password was rotated. THIS IS THE SIGNAL a credential consumer needs when `password_rotation_enabled` is true on that user: the payload never carries the password, so the receiver must refetch with `rotate_database_user_password`. Subscribing to it is what makes automatic rotation safe rather than breaking.

Requires `webhook_endpoints:update` (owner or admin).

subscribed_events.description: REPLACES the whole subscription list - include everything the endpoint should keep receiving

tools.name: delete_webhook_endpoint
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: delete a webhook endpoint. Its delivery history goes with it and the receiver stops being told anything.

Check what it was subscribed to first (`get_webhook_endpoint`). If it carried `database_user.password_rotated` for a user with automatic rotation on, deleting this silently removes the only signal that credential's consumer gets - that consumer will break at the next rotation with nothing to explain why. Say so before proceeding.

If the goal is to receive less rather than nothing, `update_webhook_endpoint` can narrow the event list instead.

Requires `webhook_endpoints:destroy` (owner or admin). You MUST set confirm=true.

confirm.description: Must be true. The receiver stops getting events and the delivery history is removed.
